identity.title: Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences? Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs

problem.claim: Evaluate whether LLMs can infer, memorize, and follow user preferences in long-context conversations.

gap.claim: The authors state that deployed LLMs remain limited in personalizing responses to user preferences.

contributions.claim: Introduces PrefEval, a benchmark with 3,000 manually curated preference-query pairs across 20 topics, covering explicit and implicit preferences.
Benchmarks 10 open-source and proprietary LLMs across multi-session conversations up to 100k tokens, including prompting, feedback, and retrieval-augmented methods.
Reports substantial difficulty with preference following and improvement from fine-tuning on PrefEval.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present PrefEval as a resource for measuring, understanding, and enhancing proactive preference following.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that, in zero-shot settings, preference-following accuracy is below 10% at 10 turns (about 3k tokens) for most evaluated models.
The authors report that preference following continues to deteriorate in long-context conversations despite advanced prompting and retrieval methods.
The authors report that fine-tuning on PrefEval significantly improves performance.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs are widely deployed, but personalization to user preferences remains limited.
The paper introduces PrefEval, spanning 3,000 preference-query pairs, 20 topics, and explicit or implicit preferences.
It evaluates 10 open-source and proprietary models in multi-session contexts up to 100k tokens using prompting, feedback, and retrieval variants.
The authors report low zero-shot accuracy, long-context deterioration, and gains from fine-tuning.

source_observation.claim: The benchmark separates explicit and implicit preferences and evaluates both generation and classification tasks.

lessons.interpretation: Separating preference visibility and task type can reveal whether failures arise from preference inference, memory, adherence, or output format.
lessons.application: Design evaluations with explicit/implicit conditions and both behavioral generation and targeted classification measures.
lessons.exception: This decomposition may be unsuitable when the application has only one preference representation or requires exclusively end-to-end interaction quality.

source_observation.claim: The reported results track preference following across conversation lengths up to 100k tokens and show deterioration even with prompting and retrieval.

lessons.interpretation: Performance should be framed as a function of conversational context, not as a single aggregate score.
lessons.application: Report results at multiple context lengths and identify the point at which preference following degrades.
lessons.exception: A length-sensitivity analysis may be unnecessary for short-session systems with fixed, small contexts.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify model identities, dataset splits, evaluation metrics beyond the reported accuracy result, or statistical details.
The abstract does not quantify the fine-tuning improvement or establish which prompting or retrieval method performs best.
